Chapter 7: The Two Criminals—Grace in the Final Hour.
You know, there’s a certain kind of loneliness that comes with regret—especially when you’re convinced it’s too late to turn things around.
Imagine, on either side of Jesus, two men hanging on their own crosses. Both of them were criminals, condemned for the choices they’d made.
Their stories could’ve ended in silence, fading out with nothing but pain and remorse. But in those final moments, something truly unexpected takes place.
Think about someone who’s sure they’ve missed their chance. Maybe you’ve felt that way—like the mistakes are just too many, and the time is running out.
One of those men next to Jesus felt exactly that. He joined in the jeers, caught up in bitterness and regret. But the other? He had a moment of real clarity. He turned to Jesus and asked for mercy. He didn’t have a long list of good deeds to offer—just a simple, honest request: “Remember me.”
Most people assume that grace is for those who’ve earned it, that forgiveness is only for the ones who somehow deserve it. But the story of these two criminals changes all of that.
It shows us that grace isn’t about timing, or performance, or having a perfect record. It’s about a heart that’s willing to ask, even when it feels like the last possible moment.
And the response? It’s instant. Jesus promises paradise—not someday, but that very day.
So if you’ve ever felt like it’s just too late, or that you’re too far gone, here’s what you need to know: it’s never too late for grace.
The cross is where every story can be rewritten, and every ending can become a brand new beginning.
The invitation is simple—let go of the past, trust that mercy is always just within reach, and believe that no one, not even you, is beyond hope.
